typical_features 'syncope without warning' and 'palpitations before syncope' added in the Round U follow-up: syncope without prodrome (or with a very short one) and sudden palpitation immediately followed by syncope are listed among the high-risk features suggesting arrhythmic syncope (Brignole M et al., 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope, Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948, Table 5, doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037). It supports the arrhythmia CATEGORY only; it never identifies a rhythm subtype, and danger adds no score. Agent-authored, not clinician-reviewed.

typical_features 'pulse rate below 50' / 'pulse rate of 150 or more' added in Round Q: a measured CURRENT rate at the thresholds the AHA adult bradycardia/tachycardia algorithms use to suggest a rhythm cause (Panchal AR et al., 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC Part 3, Circulation 2020;142:S366-S468). Weighted like a generic physiological sign (the reduced multiplier differential.py gives tachycardia/hypotension); not a confirmatory finding and never a subtype. Agent-authored, not clinician-reviewed.

First-line for any chest pain or syncope; look for ST elevation/depression, new T-wave inversion, or signs of right heart strain (PE).
Elevated in myocardial injury; a single normal troponin early after symptom onset does not exclude ACS.
High sensitivity, low specificity for PE/DVT; most useful to rule out PE in a low pre-test-probability patient, not to rule it in.
Definitive imaging for suspected pulmonary embolism when D-dimer is positive or pre-test probability is high.
Definitive imaging for suspected aortic dissection; order emergently if tearing pain with pulse/BP differential.
Elevated lactate suggests tissue hypoperfusion; used to risk-stratify suspected sepsis severity.
Confirms meningitis (CSF pleocytosis) or subarachnoid hemorrhage (xanthochromia) when CT head is negative but suspicion remains high.
First-line for suspected stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or altered mental status of unclear cause.
Mandatory in any female of childbearing age with abdominal pain before further imaging or medication decisions.
Combined with glucose and ABG to confirm diabetic ketoacidosis (ketosis + metabolic acidosis + hyperglycemia).
Elevated 3x upper limit supports acute pancreatitis; imaging still needed to assess severity/complications.
Pyuria/nitrites support UTI; also screens for hematuria (stone) and glucose/ketones (metabolic causes).
For any chest pain, first exclude ACS, aortic dissection, and PE before considering benign causes (GERD, musculoskeletal). Obtain vital signs and ECG early.

Assess for peritoneal signs (acute abdomen) first. In any female of childbearing age, exclude ectopic pregnancy before other workup. Consider GI bleeding if hemodynamic instability or PR bleeding history.

A sudden severe ('thunderclap') headache is subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise. Fever plus headache plus neck stiffness raises meningitis. Most headaches are benign (tension, migraine) but red flags change the workup entirely.

Screen for sepsis using vital signs (tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea) before assuming a benign viral source. Identify a likely infectious source (urinary, respiratory, skin, CNS) to target further workup.
Consider PE, tension pneumothorax, and cardiac causes early, especially with sudden onset or pleuritic pain. Pulse oximetry and lung auscultation guide the next step.
Distinguish true vertigo (peripheral, e.g. BPPV) from presyncope/disequilibrium; new focal neurologic signs with dizziness suggest stroke and change the whole workup.
Use a broad differential (stroke, sepsis, DKA, electrolyte disorder, meningitis, hypoglycemia) and check point-of-care glucose immediately -- a rapidly reversible cause should never be missed.
Distinguish uncomplicated cystitis from pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain, systemic signs) since the latter needs broader workup and closer follow-up; consider nephrolithiasis if colicky flank pain.

vital_sign_red_flags are deliberately generic (apply regardless of chief complaint) so a
    dangerous vital sign is never missed just because the presenting complaint didn't obviously
    point at it; per-disease `red_flag_keywords` in knowledge/diseases/*.json stay chief-complaint-
    and symptom-scoped so safety.py only raises a disease-specific flag when the current case is
    actually plausible for that disease (per spec section 5's 'never blanket-test' requirement).
Reproductive-age female with abdominal pain -- pregnancy/ectopic pregnancy must be considered regardless of whether it has been explicitly mentioned yet.
Anticoagulant use substantially raises the risk and severity of intracranial hemorrhage presenting as headache.
Antiplatelet/anticoagulant/NSAID use raises the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
Known diabetes on glucose-lowering medication raises the prior for a glucose-related emergency (DKA or hypoglycemia) in this presentation.
Glucose-lowering medication (insulin or a sulfonylurea) known to cause hypoglycemia raises the prior for a hypoglycemic episode in this presentation, especially with reduced oral intake.

These rules only ever ADD a safety finding when the case is already plausible for that diagnosis (chief-complaint-tag-gated, same as the symptom/vital-sign red flags in critical_conditions.json) -- never a blanket check across unrelated presentations (spec section 5's 'never blanket-test' requirement applies here too).
